newsitem.title: USA: Inflation sightings as common as Elvis sightings.
newsitem.headline: Inflation sightings as common as Elvis sightings.

text.p: Sightings of inflation have been as common as those of Elvis, and the latest batch of upbeat U.S. economic numbers all but guarantee that the Federal Reserve will keep its hands off interest rates next week.
It amounts to a whole lot of good news for the stock market.
Wall Street in the past week got its first glimpse of how things are shaping up early in the third quarter.
Producer prices in July fell 0.1 percent for a record seventh straight month and consumer prices inched up a marginal 0.2 percent.
In another report, retail sales rose 0.6 percent after a 0.7 percent rise in June, showing that consumers were back in the shopping malls and spending moderately.
Just a week ago, investors were on pins and needles on concern that stronger economic growth could spur the Fed to raise rates for the second time this year.
Higher interest rates can stun stocks.

Last March, the Fed raised short-term rates by a quarter percentage point on the central bank's perception that inflation was brewing in the ecomomy. The first hike in more than two years in rates sent the Dow Jones industrial average plunging 700 points. The Fed has since held the line on rates.
Market sentiment had shifted on news that the economy created 316,000 new jobs in July, far outpacing forecasts for 200,000.

Another report showed that prices paid by manufacturers rose sharply, reawakening latent inflation jitters. But the new data on inflation reconfirmed that there's still smooth sailing on the price front.
The lack of inflation pressures, which is keeping a lid on interest rates, has been a powerful force in what has been described as the Greatest Bull Market in history.
The pessimists are now scratching their heads, amazed that the moderately accelerating growth, low inflation scenario was still intact.

The Bad News Bears have been saying for the past 2-1/2 years that the market may not be able to sustain its high levels because inflation will eventually find its way back into the economy, which could hurt corporate profits.
The inflation story has stayed perfect, thanks to a strong dollar, depressed commodity prices and big productivity gains by companies and their workers.
For investors, it was just another in a series of inflation scares, as strong economic growth begets fears of inflation.

"It seems to be part of the American character to get nervous when things are going too well," says David Ranson, president of H.C. Wainwright & Co., a Boston-based consulting firm. "Unfortunately for pessimists, they will have to learn to live with the good times."
The Fed's interest-rate-setting body -- the Federal Reserve Open Market Committee -- meets Tuesday to weigh the economy and the betting is that it will hold the line on interest rates.
"The Fed doesn't have any justification for raising rates, at all, and the central bank seems to agree half way since it has only allowed a rise of only one quarter point," Ranson said.
He believes that interest rates should actually be coming down as a result of a lack of inflation, but the Fed is "resisting a cut as long as it possibly can."
But some experts reckon that the market may be entering a new "worry phase" after its spectacular run over the last 2-1/2 years.
So far this year, the Dow has gained more than 20 percent after jumping 26 percent in 1996 and 33.5 percent in 1995.

"Investors have gotten used to a linear direction for the stock market, and the minute it becomes less than linear, then they'll start to question whether the next economic report will be the one that will make them throw in the towel," said John Geraghty at North American Equity Services, a consulting firm.

He said the new breed of investors who have been dabbling in fast-rising stocks can only relate to a market that has marched upward relentlessly and most of them would be unfamiliar with a big price reversal.

"We have a generation of traders who have not seen a really serious snap-back," he said. "They've heard stories about market plunges in 1929 and 1987 but most of them have not had to relate to anything more than a technical correction."
Geraghty said that as long as stocks keep going higher, investors will be comfortable the market can only go even higher.

"But the problem for people will develop when the market starts to back and fill, and comes off a bit, then stabilizes and again comes off its highs," he said. "That's when investors will get nervous because the trend is no longer one-way and the market is no longer easy."
Some analysts have been calling for a correction for some time, and they reckoned that the market would emerge even stronger for having undergone a reversal.
In the long-run, a correction would be welcomed although, they admit that, in the short-term, it would induce some panic and confusion among investors.
In late afternoon trading Friday, the Dow index was off 119.86 points at 7,822.17 as the market consolidated its summer-long rally of nearly 880 points. For the week, it was off about 209 points.
